entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Azorubine (carmoisine) is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent red shade.
entries.expanded_summary: Azorubine (carmoisine) is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent red shade. It is a manufactured dye rather than a colour extracted from a food or plant.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for a stable red colour in foods and drinks.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Chlorophyll is the green pigment plants use to capture light for photosynthesis.
entries.expanded_summary: Chlorophyll is the green pigment plants use to capture light for photosynthesis. As a food colour it is obtained from edible plant material and concentrated.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Extracted from green plant material, then refined to concentrate chlorophyll pigments.
entries.fact_1_copy: Chlorophyll is naturally present in leafy vegetables and other green plants.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to give or restore green colour.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with an existing material — natural or manufactured — and deliberately transforms it using processes such as heating, roasting, oxidation, hydrolysis, neutralisation or other controlled treatment. The starting material can be materially changed in colour, structure or food-technology behaviour.
entries.tile_summary: This brown colour is made in a controlled factory process — it is not simply the caramel you get by browning sugar in a kitchen.
entries.expanded_summary: Caramel III (150c) is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates. Unlike kitchen caramelisation alone, this additive is produced as a colour ingredient. Caramel III is the ammonia-caramel type: carbohydrates are heated with ammonium compounds (not sulphites).
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by heated carbohydrates in the presence of ammonium compounds but not sulphite compounds, creating a complex mixture of brown colour compounds.
entries.fact_1_copy: Ammonia caramel.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to give foods and drinks brown to dark-brown colour.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority set a lower daily limit for Caramel III because an ammonia-derived manufacturing by-product caused possible immune-system effects in animals. It found no evidence that the caramel colour itself damages genes or causes cancer. Expected exposure to another manufacturing by-product was not a concern when specification limits were met. The controls therefore focus on the composition of the manufactured colour and its by-products.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: EFSA reviews safety of caramel colours (2011)

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Annatto extracts are orange-red colour preparations made from the seeds of the tropical annatto plant, Bixa orellana.
entries.expanded_summary: Annatto extracts are orange-red colour preparations made from the seeds of the tropical annatto plant, Bixa orellana. Their main pigments are bixin and norbixin.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Prepared by extracting pigments from annatto seeds and refining the extract into oil-soluble or water-dispersible colour forms.
entries.fact_1_copy: The pigment comes from the coloured coating around annatto seeds.
entries.fact_2_copy: Commonly used for yellow-orange to red-orange colour.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Lutein is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow colouring.
entries.expanded_summary: Lutein is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow colouring. It belongs to the same broad natural pigment family as beta-carotene and lutein.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial lutein is commonly extracted and purified from carotenoid-rich plant material such as marigold flowers.
entries.fact_1_copy: A xanthophyll carotenoid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for yellow colouring where permitted.

entries.consumer_display_name: Anthocyanins or Grape skin extract or Blackcurrant extract
entries.entry_title: Anthocyanins or Grape skin extract or Blackcurrant extract (163)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Anthocyanins are the red, purple and blue pigments naturally present in many fruits and vegetables.
entries.expanded_summary: Anthocyanins are the red, purple and blue pigments naturally present in many fruits and vegetables. Schedule 8 also names grape skin and blackcurrant extracts as forms of this colour family.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Extracted and concentrated from anthocyanin-rich plant material such as grape skins or blackcurrants.
entries.fact_1_copy: Anthocyanins are responsible for many red, purple and blue colours in berries, grapes and other plants.
entries.fact_2_copy: Their visible colour can shift with acidity, which is why the same pigment family can look red, purple or blue.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Elemental gold used as a decorative metallic colour where permitted.
entries.expanded_summary: Elemental gold used as a decorative metallic colour where permitted.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Highly purified gold is processed into leaf, flakes or powder for food decoration.
entries.fact_1_copy: Primarily decorative rather than a flavour or preservative ingredient.
entries.fact_2_copy: The additive is elemental gold prepared in a form suitable for decorative food use.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Benzoic acid is the parent acid in the benzoate preservative family.
entries.expanded_summary: Benzoic acid is the parent acid in the benzoate preservative family. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade benzoic acid is generally manufactured by chemical oxidation of aromatic starting materials and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Small amounts occur naturally in some fruits and fermented foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Works best as a preservative in acidic foods and drinks.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sulphur dioxide is the gaseous parent compound of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.expanded_summary: Sulphur dioxide is the gaseous parent compound of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially as a purified inorganic gas, commonly by burning sulphur or processing sulphur-containing materials.
entries.fact_1_copy: Acts as a preservative and antioxidant, and can also help control browning.
entries.fact_2_copy: Sulphur dioxide and sulphite salts can interconvert depending on pH and processing conditions.
entries.evidence_copy: In Australia and New Zealand, added sulphites at 10 milligrams per kilogram or more must be declared so sulphite-sensitive consumers can identify them. The local food regulator considers a general risk at current food levels unlikely because the former safety limit was based on weak evidence. More recent European modelling still found the smallest safety margins in high consumers, with wine, other drinks, meat preparations and dried fruit making important contributions. The finding is specific to exposure and susceptibility, rather than a general warning for everyone.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: Sulphites (updated 2025-11-26)
entries.evidence_source_2_link_label: European food-safety authority: Update of dietary exposure to sulphur dioxide-sulphites E220-228 (2025)

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium bisulphite is a potassium bisulphite form in the sulphite preservative family.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium bisulphite is a potassium bisulphite form in the sulphite preservative family.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting sulphur dioxide with a potassium alkali under controlled conditions.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for preservation and antioxidant effects.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can generate sulphur dioxide-related species in food.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium nitrate is an inorganic nitrate salt.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium nitrate is an inorganic nitrate salt. In foods it is associated mainly with curing and preservation, particularly in meat processing.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially as a purified inorganic nitrate salt from mineral or chemical starting materials.
entries.fact_1_copy: Nitrite and nitrate chemistry is used to control microbes and help develop characteristic cured-meat colour and flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: This is a nitrate salt; nitrate can be converted to nitrite under some curing conditions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Lactic acid is an organic acid produced naturally by lactic-acid bacteria during fermentation and also formed in normal metabolism.
entries.expanded_summary: Lactic acid is an organic acid produced naturally by lactic-acid bacteria during fermentation and also formed in normal metabolism. In food manufacturing it is widely used to acidify or control pH.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade lactic acid is commonly produced by fermenting sugars with selected microorganisms, followed by purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: It is associated with fermented foods such as yoghurt, pickles and sourdough.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an acid, acidity regulator and sometimes for preservation.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Malic acid is a tart organic acid naturally present in apples and many other fruits.
entries.expanded_summary: Malic acid is a tart organic acid naturally present in apples and many other fruits. Food-grade malic acid is used to add acidity and a lingering sour taste.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade malic acid is commonly manufactured from maleic or fumaric acid, although malic acid also occurs naturally in fruit.
entries.fact_1_copy: A major contributor to the tartness of apples.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an acid and acidity regulator, especially where a sustained sour note is useful.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Ascorbyl palmitate is a fat-soluble derivative of vitamin C made by linking ascorbic acid to palmitic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Ascorbyl palmitate is a fat-soluble derivative of vitamin C made by linking ascorbic acid to palmitic acid. That modification helps the antioxidant work in fatty foods and oils.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying ascorbic acid with palmitic acid, then purifying the resulting fat-soluble compound.
entries.fact_1_copy: Ordinary ascorbic acid is water-soluble; attaching a fatty-acid group makes this form more compatible with fats.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an antioxidant, especially in fat-containing foods.
entries.evidence_copy: A United Nations food-additive expert committee reviewed 304 in 2025. It found that the additive is rapidly split into vitamin C and palmitic acid before much intact material reaches the bloodstream. The committee therefore removed the former numerical daily limit. Its formal finding of an ‘acceptable daily intake not specified’ means the assessed uses did not need a numerical cap; it does not mean unlimited use.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: United Nations food-additive expert committee: Vitamin C palmitate INS 304 evaluation (2025)

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Propyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid designed to work as an antioxidant in fats and oils.
entries.expanded_summary: Propyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid designed to work as an antioxidant in fats and oils. The propyl group makes the molecule more compatible with fatty ingredients than gallic acid itself.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by chemically esterifying gallic acid with the corresponding propyl alcohol and purifying the product.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to slow oxidative rancidity in fats and oils.
entries.fact_2_copy: Built from gallic-acid chemistry but manufactured as a more fat-soluble ester.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) is a synthetic mixture of phenolic antioxidant compounds.
entries.expanded_summary: Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) is a synthetic mixture of phenolic antioxidant compounds. It is used in small amounts to slow oxidative rancidity and protect flavour or shelf life in fat-containing foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled organic chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps protect fats and oils from oxidation.
entries.evidence_copy: The World Health Organization's cancer-hazard agency classifies BHA as a possible cancer hazard, based largely on high-dose animal findings including changes in the rat forestomach. A hazard classification does not estimate risk from the amount used in food. Europe's food-safety authority later found no evidence of gene damage, considered the forestomach findings of doubtful relevance to people and set an exposure-based safety limit. Estimated dietary intake was generally below that limit.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of BHA E320 (2011)
entries.evidence_source_2_link_label: World Health Organization cancer-hazard agency: Agents classified by the IARC Monographs (classification list)

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Ammonium lactate is the ammonium salt of lactic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium lactate is the ammonium salt of lactic acid. It keeps the familiar lactic-acid chemistry but in a less acidic salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising lactic acid — commonly produced by fermentation of sugars — with a ammonium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from lactic acid, the acid associated with many fermented foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt, can regulate acidity, retain moisture, firm texture or support preservation.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Tartaric acid is a naturally occurring fruit acid strongly associated with grapes and wine.
entries.expanded_summary: Tartaric acid is a naturally occurring fruit acid strongly associated with grapes and wine. Commercial food-grade tartaric acid is often recovered from wine-making by-products.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commonly recovered and purified from potassium hydrogen tartrate and other tartaric-acid salts formed during grape and wine processing; synthetic routes also exist.
entries.fact_1_copy: Grapes are a particularly rich natural source.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an acid and acidity regulator and in some raising-agent systems.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium phosphates are a family of potassium salts of phosphoric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium phosphates are a family of potassium salts of phosphoric acid. Schedule 8 groups several mono-, di- or tribasic forms under the same additive number.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting purified phosphoric acid with potassium-containing mineral or chemical bases and controlling the degree of neutralisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Different phosphate forms have different acidity, solubility and buffering behaviour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the form, phosphates can regulate acidity, act in raising systems, stabilise texture or bind water.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority assessed potassium phosphates as part of total phosphorus exposure from food and supplements. Estimated exposure exceeded the group safety value in some younger age groups. That value was designed for healthy people and does not apply to people with moderate or severe kidney impairment. Code 340 identifies one phosphate source; it cannot show a person's total dietary exposure.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates E338-341, E343, E450-452 (2019)

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium malate is a potassium salt of malic acid, the tart fruit acid associated with apples and many other fruits.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium malate is a potassium salt of malic acid, the tart fruit acid associated with apples and many other fruits.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified malic acid with a potassium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from malic acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for acidity control, buffering or mineral delivery depending on the salt.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Ammonium adipates is a ammonium salt of adipic acid, a manufactured dicarboxylic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium adipates is a ammonium salt of adipic acid, a manufactured dicarboxylic acid.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising adipic acid with a ammonium-containing base and purifying the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from adipic acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for acidity control or related processing functions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Ammonium citrate and triammonium citrate are ammonium salts of citric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium citrate and triammonium citrate are ammonium salts of citric acid. They combine citrate's acidity-control and metal-binding chemistry with ammonium ions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by neutralising fermentation-produced citric acid with ammonia under controlled conditions.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from citric acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for acidity control, buffering or sequestration depending on the application.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium alginate is the potassium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium alginate is the potassium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Brown seaweed is washed, extracted and processed to isolate alginate; the required acid or salt form is then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Alginate is a structural polysaccharide in brown algae.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to thicken, stabilise or form gels depending on the form and food.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Processed eucheuma seaweed is a less-refined carrageenan-rich ingredient made directly from certain red seaweeds.
entries.expanded_summary: Processed eucheuma seaweed is a less-refined carrageenan-rich ingredient made directly from certain red seaweeds. It retains more of the seaweed's insoluble material than purified carrageenan.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Eucheuma/Kappaphycus seaweed is washed and treated with alkali, then dried and milled rather than fully extracting the carrageenan.
entries.fact_1_copy: It is processed seaweed containing carrageenan, not purified carrageenan alone.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for thickening, stabilising and gelling.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority assessed 407a with food-grade carrageenan because their structures and behaviour in the body are similar. Adverse animal studies often cited in this debate used degraded carrageenan such as poligeenan, a much smaller polymer produced under extreme acid and heat conditions and not authorised as a food additive. The authority still requested better molecular-weight and exposure data for the food-grade group, supporting both the distinction and continued specification control.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of carrageenan E407 and processed Eucheuma seaweed E407a (2018)

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Xanthan gum is a high-molecular-weight carbohydrate made by bacteria during fermentation.
entries.expanded_summary: Xanthan gum is a high-molecular-weight carbohydrate made by bacteria during fermentation. It can thicken liquids strongly at low concentrations and remains effective across a wide range of acidity and temperature.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by fermenting sugars with Xanthomonas bacteria, then recovering, purifying, drying and milling the xanthan polymer.
entries.fact_1_copy: It gives viscosity even at low levels and can help suspend particles.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a thickener, stabiliser and texture modifier.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Glycerol helps hold moisture and carry flavour — and the number 422 alone will not tell you whether it came from plant oil, animal fat or a synthetic route.
entries.expanded_summary: Glycerol is a small, sweet-tasting alcohol that forms the backbone of fats and oils. In foods it is useful for holding moisture, carrying flavours and controlling texture.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial glycerol is commonly recovered and purified from vegetable-oil or animal-fat processing and biodiesel production; synthetic routes also exist.
entries.fact_1_copy: Every triglyceride fat molecule contains a glycerol backbone.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a humectant, solvent, carrier, sweet-tasting ingredient or texture modifier.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number does not reveal whether the commercial glycerol came from plant oil, animal fat or a synthetic route.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Pectin is a plant carbohydrate that helps bind the cell walls of fruits and vegetables.
entries.expanded_summary: Pectin is a plant carbohydrate that helps bind the cell walls of fruits and vegetables. Commercial pectin is commonly extracted from citrus peel or apple pomace and is prized for its ability to form gels.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by hot-acid extraction of pectin-rich plant by-products such as citrus peel or apple pomace, followed by purification and drying.
entries.fact_1_copy: Pectin is the natural gelling material behind many jams and fruit preserves.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a gelling agent, thickener and stabiliser.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Polyphosphates are condensed phosphate salts in which phosphate units are linked together; this Schedule 8 number covers several sodium and/or potassium forms.
entries.expanded_summary: Polyphosphates are condensed phosphate salts in which phosphate units are linked together; this Schedule 8 number covers several sodium and/or potassium forms. Compared with simple phosphates, their chain structure gives different water-binding, buffering and texture effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by heating and condensing purified phosphate salts under controlled conditions, then forming the required sodium or potassium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Longer chains or glassy forms of phosphate.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can act in raising systems, moisture retention, emulsification, sequestration or texture control depending on the food.
entries.evidence_copy: After digestion, 452 contributes to the body's total phosphorus. Europe's food-safety authority therefore assessed it with other phosphate additives and phosphorus from the rest of the diet. The group safety value protected healthy people, but supplements alone could exceed it and the value did not cover people with moderate or severe kidney impairment. An ingredient list can identify 452 as one contributor, but cannot show a person's total phosphorus exposure.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates E338-341, E343, E450-452 (2019)

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose.
entries.expanded_summary: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose. Introducing both methyl and hydroxypropyl groups changes cellulose from an insoluble plant fibre into a material with useful thickening, film-forming or stabilising behaviour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with purified plant cellulose, which is reacted under controlled conditions to introduce both methyl and hydroxypropyl groups; the product is then washed and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant cellulose, commonly from wood pulp or cotton-derived material.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a thickener, stabiliser, film former or texture modifier depending on the derivative.

entries.consumer_display_name: Lactic and fatty acid esters of glycerol
entries.entry_title: Lactic and fatty acid esters of glycerol (472b)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Lactic and fatty acid esters of glycerol are emulsifiers made by adding lactic acid-derived groups to mono- and diglyceride-type fat molecules.
entries.expanded_summary: Lactic and fatty acid esters of glycerol are emulsifiers made by adding lactic acid-derived groups to mono- and diglyceride-type fat molecules. The modification changes how the molecules interact with dough, fat and water.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made from glycerol/fatty-acid materials plus lactic acid-derived components through controlled esterification; fatty-acid sources can be plant or animal.
entries.fact_1_copy: Built on glycerol and fatty acids, the same broad building blocks found in edible fats.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as emulsifiers and texture/process aids, with some forms particularly important in bakery applications.

entries.consumer_display_name: Polyglycerol esters of interesterified ricinoleic acid
entries.entry_title: Polyglycerol esters of interesterified ricinoleic acid (476)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Chocolate makers use PGPR (476) to help chocolate flow smoothly. Its fatty-acid building blocks come from castor oil.
entries.expanded_summary: PGPR (polyglycerol esters of interesterified ricinoleic acid) is a fat-phase emulsifier. Its characteristic fatty acid comes from castor-oil chemistry. Food makers use it especially to manage flow and viscosity in chocolate and other fat-based coatings.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Ricinoleic-acid-rich material from castor oil is polymerised/interesterified and then esterified with polyglycerol.
entries.fact_1_copy: The characteristic fatty acid originates from castor-oil chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used especially to control flow and viscosity in chocolate and fat-based coatings.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority found that 476 is broken down in the gut. It found no evidence of gene damage or cancer and no significant adverse effects in the available human studies. The authority raised the daily safety limit from 7.5 to 25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, and estimated intake remained below that level. This conclusion assumes food-grade material that meets the required impurity limits.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of polyglycerol polyricinoleate E476 (2017)

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Sorbitan tristearate is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived sorbitan and stearic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Sorbitan tristearate is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived sorbitan and stearic acid. The molecule carries three stearic-acid groups, which tunes how it behaves in fats and emulsions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by dehydrating sorbitol to sorbitan and esterifying it with stearic acid; the fatty-acid starting material can come from plant or animal fats.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to emulsify and stabilise fat-containing foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: The final ingredient is manufactured even though its fatty-acid feedstock may originate from edible fats or oils.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium chloride is a simple mineral salt of potassium and chloride.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium chloride is a simple mineral salt of potassium and chloride.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from purified potash/mineral salt sources or chemical crystallisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Can provide saltiness, potassium and processing functions; it is often used where sodium chloride is being partly replaced.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium sulphate is an inorganic potassium sulphate salt.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium sulphate is an inorganic potassium sulphate salt.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from potash minerals or produced by chemical conversion and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a mineral salt and processing ingredient where permitted.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium hydroxide, also known as slaked lime, is an inorganic alkaline material.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium hydroxide, also known as slaked lime, is an inorganic alkaline material. It is alkaline and is used for firming, pH control, nixtamalisation and other processing steps.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by adding water to calcium oxide produced by heating limestone.
entries.fact_1_copy: A strongly or moderately basic calcium-containing compound used for processing rather than flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its technical name can sound severe because concentrated material is reactive; food use is controlled and application-specific.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with animal or insect material. The target substance is separated from that material and then cleaned, refined or converted into a stable food-grade form.
entries.tile_summary: Bone phosphate is a calcium-phosphate-rich material obtained from animal bones after removal of organic matter.
entries.expanded_summary: Bone phosphate is a calcium-phosphate-rich material obtained from animal bones after removal of organic matter. Its composition is dominated by mineral calcium phosphates.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by cleaning, degreasing and heat-processing animal bones, then grinding/refining the remaining mineral material.
entries.fact_1_copy: Animal bone mineral.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an anticaking, mineral or processing material where permitted.
entries.fact_3_copy: The animal origin may matter for dietary or ethical preferences.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium aluminium silicate is an inorganic calcium aluminosilicate.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium aluminium silicate is an inorganic calcium aluminosilicate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured from purified calcium, aluminium and silica sources.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used mainly as an anticaking or carrier material.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium gluconate is the sodium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium gluconate is the sodium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose. The gluconate part is highly water-compatible and can bind minerals.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from fermentation/oxidation-derived gluconic acid followed by neutralisation with a sodium-containing source.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glucose-derived gluconic acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the mineral, used for mineral delivery, acidity control, sequestration, colour stabilisation or processing.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: L-glutamic acid is an amino acid that occurs naturally in proteins and also as free glutamate in foods such as tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms.
entries.expanded_summary: L-glutamic acid is an amino acid that occurs naturally in proteins and also as free glutamate in foods such as tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms. Free glutamate is strongly associated with umami, the savoury taste.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade glutamic acid is commonly produced by fermenting carbohydrate starting materials with selected microorganisms, then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glutamate is widespread in ordinary foods and in the body's proteins and metabolism.
entries.fact_2_copy: Free glutamate activates umami taste receptors.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as a flavour enhancer and acidity-related ingredient.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Disodium 5′-guanylate is the disodium salt of a guanosine nucleotide.
entries.expanded_summary: Disodium 5′-guanylate is the disodium salt of a guanosine nucleotide. These nucleotide flavour enhancers strongly boost savoury taste, especially when used together with glutamate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade nucleotide salts are commonly produced from microbial fermentation or enzymatic processing of biological nucleotide material, then purified and converted to the sodium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Guanylate and inosinate can amplify umami far more strongly when combined with glutamate than when used alone.
entries.fact_2_copy: Related nucleotide compounds occur naturally in foods and cells.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as flavour enhancers in savoury foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: L-Leucine is an essential amino acid found naturally in dietary proteins.
entries.expanded_summary: L-Leucine is an essential amino acid found naturally in dietary proteins. As a food additive it can be used for technological functions such as flavour, nutrient formulation or powder handling.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial L-leucine is commonly produced by microbial fermentation and purified by crystallisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: A normal amino-acid component of protein foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Leucine is an essential amino acid, although its role as an additive depends on the product formulation.
entries.fact_3_copy: Can be used in specialised flavour, nutrition or processing applications.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Oxidised polyethylene is a modified polyethylene wax.
entries.expanded_summary: Oxidised polyethylene is a modified polyethylene wax. Controlled oxidation adds oxygen-containing groups to the polymer surface, changing its hardness and coating behaviour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Polyethylene is manufactured from ethylene and then deliberately oxidised under controlled conditions to produce the food-grade wax.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a glazing or coating agent.
entries.fact_2_copy: A synthetic polymer wax rather than a natural wax such as beeswax or carnauba.

entries.source_profile_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
entries.tile_summary: Propane is a small hydrocarbon gas widely used as a fuel but also purified for specialised food-propellant use.
entries.expanded_summary: Propane is a small hydrocarbon gas widely used as a fuel but also purified for specialised food-propellant use.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Separated and purified from natural-gas and petroleum-refining streams.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a propellant where permitted; it is volatile and leaves the product as gas after dispensing.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms.
entries.expanded_summary: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms. The result is intensely sweet but metabolised very differently from ordinary sugar.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from sucrose through a controlled multi-step chlorination and purification process.
entries.fact_1_copy: Sucrose — ordinary table sugar — is the structural starting point.
entries.fact_2_copy: About 600 times sweeter than sucrose.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used for intense sweetness and is relatively stable during many cooking and processing conditions.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority kept the daily safety limit for sucralose at 15 milligrams per kilogram of body weight in 2026 and found estimated exposure from currently authorised uses below it in every population group. The same review could not support a proposed extension to more fine bakery products because the many possible baking times and temperatures left a question about forming chlorinated compounds. The reassuring conclusion covers current authorised uses; the unresolved issue concerns a proposed broader high-temperature use.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of sucralose E955 and proposed bakery extension (2026)

entries.consumer_display_name: Maltitol and maltitol syrup or hydrogenated glucose syrup
entries.entry_title: Maltitol and maltitol syrup or hydrogenated glucose syrup (965)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Maltitol and maltitol syrup are sugar-alcohol sweeteners produced from starch-derived maltose or glucose syrups.
entries.expanded_summary: Maltitol and maltitol syrup are sugar-alcohol sweeteners produced from starch-derived maltose or glucose syrups. They provide bulk and texture as well as sweetness.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starch is broken down to maltose/glucose-rich syrup and then hydrogenated; crystalline maltitol or mixed hydrogenated glucose syrup is purified for food use.
entries.fact_1_copy: Usually starch-derived carbohydrate syrup.
entries.fact_2_copy: Maltitol is less sweet than sucrose but much closer to sugar in bulk and texture than intense sweeteners are.
entries.fact_3_copy: Widely used in sugar-reduced confectionery and fillings because it supplies body as well as sweetness.
entries.evidence_copy: Maltitol is not fully absorbed, so larger servings can draw water into the bowel and be fermented, causing bloating or loose stools. A United Nations food-additive expert committee did not consider a numerical toxicological limit necessary for its assessed uses. Australia and New Zealand require relevant foods containing polyols to state that excess consumption may have a laxative effect. Portion size and the combined amount of polyols matter more than one occurrence of 965 on a label.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: Warning and advisory statements (updated 2025-11-26)
entries.evidence_source_2_link_label: United Nations food-additive expert committee: Maltitol INS 965 evaluation (1993)

entries.source_profile_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.
entries.tile_summary: Alpha-amylase is an enzyme that breaks starch into smaller sugars and dextrins.
entries.expanded_summary: Alpha-amylase is an enzyme that breaks starch into smaller sugars and dextrins. The enzyme family occurs naturally across plants, animals and microorganisms; food-grade preparations are commonly produced with selected microbes.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food enzymes are usually produced by controlled fermentation with bacteria or fungi, followed by filtration and purification of the enzyme preparation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Cuts alpha-1,4 bonds in starch, reducing viscosity and producing smaller carbohydrates.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used in baking, brewing, starch processing and other applications where starch needs to be broken down.
entries.fact_3_copy: An enzyme is a protein catalyst, not a conventional small-molecule additive.

entries.tile_summary: Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) is a synthetic water-soluble polymer.
entries.expanded_summary: Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) is a synthetic water-soluble polymer. In food and beverage processing it is used mainly for specialised binding, stabilising or clarification roles rather than as a source of nutrition.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by polymerising N-vinyl-2-pyrrolidone under controlled conditions and purifying the polymer.
entries.fact_1_copy: A synthetic polymer made from repeating vinylpyrrolidone units.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used in specialised applications including clarification/stabilisation and as a carrier or processing aid depending on permission.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Enzyme-treated starches is starch whose molecular size or branching has been changed with starch-active enzymes.
entries.expanded_summary: Enzyme-treated starches is starch whose molecular size or branching has been changed with starch-active enzymes. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes enzymatic hydrolysis or restructuring, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Acetylated distarch adipate is cross-linked starch with acetyl groups and adipate bridges.
entries.expanded_summary: Acetylated distarch adipate is cross-linked starch with acetyl groups and adipate bridges. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes acetylation plus adipate cross-linking, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Triacetin is glycerol triacetate — a molecule made by attaching three acetic-acid-derived groups to glycerol.
entries.expanded_summary: Triacetin is glycerol triacetate — a molecule made by attaching three acetic-acid-derived groups to glycerol. It is used mainly as a solvent, carrier and texture/plasticising ingredient.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying glycerol with acetic acid or acetic anhydride, then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glycerol plus acetate groups.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a carrier for flavours, a humectant/solvent or a plasticiser in coatings and gum bases.

entries.consumer_display_name: Monk fruit extract or luo han guo extract
entries.entry_title: Monk fruit extract or luo han guo extract
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Monk fruit extract, or luo han guo extract, is an intensely sweet botanical extract from the fruit of Siraitia grosvenorii.
entries.expanded_summary: Monk fruit extract, or luo han guo extract, is an intensely sweet botanical extract from the fruit of Siraitia grosvenorii. Its sweetness comes mainly from mogrosides such as mogroside V.
entries.source_preparation_copy: The fruit is water-extracted; the sweet mogrosides are then filtered, concentrated and purified, often using adsorption/resin steps.
entries.fact_1_copy: Monk fruit / luo han guo.
entries.fact_2_copy: Mogrosides are intensely sweet, allowing small amounts of extract to replace some sugar sweetness.
entries.fact_3_copy: FSANZ lists this additive by name without a numeric additive code.
